name: Collagen induction therapy

card.summary: Microneedling: controlled skin punctures meant to trigger collagen repair; the best-studied use is scars, with more modest evidence for wrinkles and texture.
card.aka: Microneedling, dermarolling, skin needling, percutaneous collagen induction (PCI)
card.note: Non-clinical settings with poor infection control have been linked to blood-borne infection outbreaks when combined with blood-derived products.

quick.overview:
Collagen induction therapy, usually called microneedling, uses a roller, stamp or motorised pen studded with fine needles to puncture the skin many times. The aim is to provoke a wound-healing response that produces new collagen and elastin without removing the epidermis.

It is used for acne and other scars, stretch marks, fine lines, skin laxity and general skin texture. Published studies, mostly small or retrospective, report improvement in scars and some photoaging, while larger controlled evidence is more limited.
quick.mechanism: Needle punctures create micro-channels and tiny injuries in the dermis. Proponents and authors of the early clinical papers describe a healing cascade of inflammation, fibroblast activity and new collagen deposition over weeks to months, with the epidermis left largely intact.
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, swelling, pinpoint bleeding and temporary irritation. Infections, pigment changes and scarring have been described in complication reviews, and public-health authorities have warned about blood-borne infection when needling is paired with blood-derived products in unregulated settings. Professional microneedling devices are regulated as medical devices in the US; home devices vary widely.

lead: Collagen induction therapy (CIT), widely known as microneedling, dermarolling or skin needling, is a cosmetic procedure in which a device bearing fine needles repeatedly punctures the skin to create controlled micro-injuries [1][11]. The aim is to trigger the skin's own repair response, with new collagen and elastin laid down over the following weeks and months, without removing the outer skin layer as ablative lasers and deep peels do [2][3][16].

For appearance, the practice is used on atrophic acne scars, surgical and burn scars, stretch marks, fine lines, enlarged pores, uneven texture and mild skin laxity, and it has been paired with topical products, platelet-rich plasma (PRP), radiofrequency energy and, in hair-loss circles, minoxidil [11][16][18][26]. In looksmaxxing communities it appears most often as a skin-quality and scar tool, and as an add-on to hairline, brow and under-eye routines, using home rollers, stamps and pens as well as clinic devices [29][30][31].

The published literature runs from the original percutaneous collagen induction papers of the late 2000s to narrative reviews, a meta-analysis on stretch marks and randomized trials of combined treatments [2][16][17][18]. Reviews describe the results as encouraging for scars, striae and rhytides, and also note that many studies are small or uncontrolled and that devices and protocols vary widely [16][18]. Public-health reports have documented serious infections when needling was combined with blood-derived products in unlicensed settings [11].

chain: Fine needles create controlled micro-channels in the dermis
Wound-healing cascade builds new collagen and elastin over weeks to months
Shallower acne scars and stretch marks, smoother texture and finer lines
angle.text: People use microneedling to soften the look of acne scars, stretch marks and fine lines and to improve skin texture, usually in a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. Clinic devices and home rollers are both used, and results are described as building gradually over months.

paras: Collagen induction therapy covers any technique that wounds the skin with fine needles in order to remodel it. The main device families are hand-held rollers (a drum studded with needles), stamps (a flat head pressed down repeatedly), motorised pens with disposable cartridges and radiofrequency microneedling heads that deliver heat energy through insulated needles [1][19]. Needle lengths are commonly described as running from a fraction of a millimetre to about 3 mm, with shallow settings used for the delicate skin around the eyes and longer settings for scars and stretch marks on thicker skin [1][18].

Grokipedia reports that clinic sessions typically involve numbing cream, several passes in different directions and a series of three to six treatments spaced weeks apart, with visible changes building over three to six months; these specifics come from a single AI-generated page and vary between sources [1]. Peer-reviewed practical guides describe a similar pattern of pretreatment, treatment endpoint and aftercare chosen by the clinician [18].

Proponents and reviewers describe a staged healing response. Needle punctures release platelet-derived growth factors and cytokines, fibroblasts migrate into the area and produce new collagen and elastin, and the matrix is gradually remodelled over months [1][2][16]. Because the epidermis is perforated rather than stripped, the authors of the early papers argued that healing is quick and that the risk of pigment disturbance is lower than with ablative lasers or peels [2][4].

A 2017 comprehensive review notes that the microwounds stimulate growth-factor release and collagen production while leaving the epidermis relatively intact, which it says helps limit adverse events [16]. The same logic underlies the use of microneedling to increase the penetration of topical products through the micro-channels, a use covered by the same review [16].

According to Grokipedia, the technique originated in the 1990s with South African plastic surgeon Desmond Fernandes, who used a tattoo-gun-like device on scars, and a roller with needles was introduced by German inventor Horst Liebl around 2000 [1]. These origin details come from one AI-generated source and are not confirmed in the peer-reviewed papers cited here.

The technique reached the plastic-surgery literature through a group publishing from the mid-2000s under the term percutaneous collagen induction. A 2008 retrospective analysis of 480 patients treated between 1997 and 2006 reported improvement of scars, wrinkles and skin laxity [2], and companion papers the same year discussed photoaging and the question of hyperpigmentation [3][4]. Further papers followed on burn scars, burn-scar contracture and striae distensae in 2008 to 2010 [5][6][7]. Grokipedia dates automated pens to around 2010 and says US regulators classified aesthetic microneedling devices as Class II in 2018 [1].

Reviews in 2017 and 2018 consolidated the field, concluding that microneedling had spread from scar treatment to rejuvenation, melasma, alopecia and drug delivery [16][18]. Later work examined combinations with radiofrequency, fillers, PRP and exosome products [19][21][22][23][24][25][26].

Atrophic acne scars are the best-established indication. The early series reported improvement in facial scars, and a 2020 evaluation of microneedling in facial scars also reported benefit [2][10]. A 2017 review of human studies lists scars and acne among the conditions where trials report efficacy [16]. Burn scars were studied in a clinical series [5], and a case report described treatment of burn-scar contracture with a pinhole method followed by collagen induction [6]. Registered trials have compared microneedling with silicone sheeting for hypertrophic scars and tested it with a filler for facial acne scars [13][15].

A 2010 report described improvement of striae distensae after percutaneous collagen induction [7]. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of eleven controlled studies (six randomized, five not) found that microneedle radiofrequency produced a significant clinical-improvement effect (standardized mean difference 0.57), and that microneedling and lasers gave comparable results, with no significant difference between them [17]. A registered trial compared collagen induction with a fractional non-ablative laser in atrophic striae [14].

Authors of the early papers presented the method as a skin-rejuvenation option for photoaged skin [3][4], and a study of upper-lip wrinkles reported benefit [9]. Reviews of facial-rejuvenation procedures describe microneedling alone and combined with PRP, radiofrequency and other products [12][26]. A randomized trial of radiofrequency microneedling with injected poly-L-lactic acid looked at facial laxity [23].
Reviews list dyschromia, melasma and enlarged pores among the proposed indications [16][18]. A 2022 systematic review of melasma treatment covers procedural options within the broader field [27].

Microneedling is also used on the scalp, usually together with a topical. A randomized placebo-controlled study examined microneedling with topical dutasteride solution for androgenetic alopecia [20], and a 2024 systematic review of androgenetic alopecia treatments covers procedural options [28]. Wikipedia notes that some studies suggest combining microneedling with minoxidil treats hair loss better than minoxidil alone [11]. Forum threads discuss needling the hairline, the brows and the beard area in the same terms [29][30].

A retrospective analysis of 480 patients treated between 1997 and 2006 reported improvement of scars, wrinkles and skin laxity with percutaneous collagen induction [2]. Related papers discussed photoaging and whether the technique avoids hyperpigmentation [3][4]. A burn-scar study [5], a striae report [7], an upper-lip wrinkle study [9] and a 2020 evaluation in facial scars [10] each reported improvement.

Review literature includes a 2017 comprehensive review whose authors concluded that microneedling appears effective and safe for scars, acne, melasma, photodamage, rejuvenation, hyperhidrosis and alopecia, and that permanent adverse events are uncommon while transient redness and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation are more commonly reported [16]. A 2018 review and practical guide reported substantial improvement of scars, striae and rhytides with limited recovery time [18]. The 2024 striae meta-analysis is described above [17], and a 2021 critical review examined radiofrequency microneedling [19].

Randomized trials of combinations include microneedling with radiofrequency plus ablative fractional laser for acne and acne scars [24], radiofrequency microneedling with poly-L-lactic acid for laxity [23], microneedling with exosome solutions for skin aging in a split-face design [21], exosomes compared with PRP in photoaged skin [22], and an exosome complex with microneedling in people with thinning hair [25]. Registered trials include silicone sheeting versus microneedling [13], collagen induction versus laser in stretch marks [14] and microneedling with a filler for acne scars [15]. Many published studies are small, uncontrolled or retrospective, and reviewers call for standardized protocols [16][18].

Expected short-term effects include redness, swelling, pinpoint bleeding and temporary discomfort [1][16]. A review of complications from aesthetic procedures lists infection and pigment change among events reported across techniques [8]. Reviews state that post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is among the more commonly reported events, and that permanent adverse events are uncommon [16].

Grokipedia lists contraindications such as active skin infection, bleeding disorders, keloid history and recent isotretinoin use, and lists tram-track scarring and allergic reactions as rare events; these come from a single AI-generated source [1].

Wikipedia reports that health authorities have raised concern about needling combined with PRP in non-medical settings. In 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health warned that such businesses could spread blood-borne infections, and in April 2024 the CDC reported three women diagnosed with HIV after vampire facials at an Albuquerque spa; about 200 other clients and partners tested negative [11]. Grokipedia also reports an October 2025 US FDA safety communication on serious complications from radiofrequency microneedling, including burns and scarring, often involving unregulated devices and non-medical operators [1].

Home rollers and stamps are sold directly to consumers, and Grokipedia says dermarollers are not FDA-authorized for over-the-counter sale while professional pens are used in clinics under medical-device rules [1]. Clinic proponents cite sterile single-use cartridges, adjustable depth and topical anaesthetic; home users cite cost and convenience [1][30]. Grokipedia states that home devices are generally limited to shallow needle lengths while clinicians use deeper settings [1].

The pairing of microneedling with PRP drawn from the client's own blood became known as a vampire facial and was popularised through celebrity and spa coverage; Wikipedia states that whether PRP adds benefit remains in question pending scientific studies [11]. Looksmaxxing posters describe using their own blood with a pen device [31].

On looksmax.org, threads cover dermarolling the under-eyes with retinoids to thicken thin skin [29], at-home scar routines using fine-needle rollers or stamps [30], pen depth for anti-ageing [31], dermarolling for the hairline, brows and under-eye lines [32][33], minoxidil with dermarolling [34], and combinations with peptides such as GHK-Cu [35]. Posters often present it as a low-cost scar and skin-quality tool, and some threads question it, including one titled as a warning [36]. The forum posts also include hygiene and aftercare advice written by lay users, which this article does not reproduce.

Related procedures include fractional lasers, chemical peels, radiofrequency devices, dermal fillers such as poly-L-lactic acid, and topical retinoids, several of which appear as comparators or partners in the trials above [14][23][24]. Exosome and PRP products are marketed as post-needling adjuncts, and trials of them are early [21][22][25].

timeline.event: Grokipedia attributes the technique to Desmond Fernandes; this is also the start of the patient series later published in 2008 [1][2].
Roller device attributed to Horst Liebl, per Grokipedia [1].
Retrospective series of 480 patients on percutaneous collagen induction published; companion papers on photoaging and hyperpigmentation appear [2][3][4].
Burn-scar and stretch-mark papers on collagen induction published [5][7].
Pilot trial of microneedling with a filler for acne scars begins [15].
Comprehensive review of microneedling published in Dermatologic Surgery; a stretch-mark trial against laser begins [14][16].
New Mexico health department warns of infection risk from needling with blood products; Grokipedia says devices were classed Class II in the US [1][11].
Critical review of radiofrequency microneedling published [19].
CDC reports three HIV diagnoses linked to a spa offering vampire facials; a meta-analysis of microneedling for striae is published [11][17].

lore.intro: Microneedling is discussed on looksmax.org and similar forums as a scar, texture, hairline and under-eye tool, often with home devices and add-on products [29][30][31].

claims.claim: Microneedling builds collagen and fades acne scars over several sessions.
claims.believers: Proponents say repeated needling triggers new collagen and softens acne scars and stretch marks; one forum guide says it is no wonder cure and that consistency is what shows results [30].
claims.experts: Retrospective series, reviews and a meta-analysis on striae report improvement, with reviewers noting small and uncontrolled studies [2][16][17].

claims.claim: Dermarolling the under-eyes with retinoids thickens thin skin and reduces the dark, grey look.
claims.believers: A poster proposes needling the area with retinoids to thicken skin so underlying colour shows less, while accepting that hollowness would remain [29].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested this under-eye protocol; general reviews describe periorbital skin as delicate and shallow settings as used there [1][16].

claims.believers: Forum replies describe deeper settings as generally better, while others say frequent 2 mm sessions may cause scarring [31].
claims.experts: Reviews describe needle depth chosen by indication and operator, and list scarring and pigment change among reported complications [8][16][18].

claims.claim: Microneedling avoids the pigmentation risk of lasers and peels.
claims.believers: Proponents say the epidermis stays largely intact, so darker skin tones can be treated.
claims.experts: The early authors argued this [4], while the 2017 review lists post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation among the more commonly reported events [16].

claims.claim: Microneedling with PRP or own blood gives superior results.
claims.believers: Users and clinics promote PRP add-ons, and one poster describes returning to his own blood with a pen [31].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says efficacy of the combination remains in question, and documents HIV infections after unregulated vampire facials [11].

claims.claim: Dermarolling restores hairline density and helps with minoxidil.
claims.believers: Forum threads describe dermarolling the hairline and combining it with minoxidil and report fuller hairline and fewer lines [32][34].
claims.experts: A randomized study tested microneedling with topical dutasteride, and a systematic review covers procedural treatments for androgenetic alopecia [20][28]; Wikipedia says some studies suggest an advantage over minoxidil alone [11].

claims.claim: Peptides and exosome products applied through the micro-channels boost results.
claims.believers: Posters discuss using GHK-Cu with microneedling [35]; clinics market exosome serums.
claims.experts: Early randomized split-face and comparison trials of exosome products with microneedling have been published, and reviewers describe the field as emerging [21][22][25].
